newsitem.title: USA: Taiwan official says U.S. bows to war game plan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan official says U.S. bows to war game plan.

text.p: Taiwan's chief representative in Washington said on Wednesday U.S. officials "fully understand" Taiwan's plan to stage war games on the eve of Hong Kong's reversion to Chinese control.

Jason Hu of the office that functions as an embassy in the absence of U.S.-Taiwanese diplomatic relations acknowledged Washington had raised questions about the exercise set for June 23 and 24. "People did ask me about this and I did seek clearance for information from home" to reply to U.S. officials, he told reporters at the National Press Club.
After Taiwan responded to U.S. concerns, "we all fully understand," Hu added. Declining to elaborate, he said he had already strayed from a practice of not disclosing his talks with U.S. officials.

The State Department voiced hope Taiwan's drills would not rekindle tension with China, which regards the island as a renegade province because it was a refuge for Nationalist troops who lost China's civil war to the communists in 1949.
Hong Kong newspaper Sing Tao Daily said on Tuesday that Beijing was planning war games of its own this month off the southeastern Fujian coast to counter Taiwan's.

"We hope both sides will continue efforts to ease tension and that they will exercise restraint, including restraint in military activities during sensitive periods," a State Department spokesman said.

If both governments went ahead with war games tensions could return to their March 1996 levels, when Beijing shook the region with menacing live-fire exercises in the Taiwan Straits off Taiwan's coast.

China said then it was warning voters in Taiwan's first presidential elections against any moves toward declaring independence. The United States responded by sending two aircraft carrier battle groups to the region in a show of support for Taiwan.
Hu, who heads the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in the United States, said the timing of Taiwan's exercise was in no way related to the Hong Kong handover at midnight on June 30.

"There's no political message, period," he said, describing the war games as routine and long-delayed. Pressed on the timing, he said there was "no better time" because political significance could always be imputed.
Delaying, he said, might conflict, for instance, with a Communist Party plenum in Beijing this summer or a planned visit to Washington later by Chinese President Jiang Zemin.

In strongly worded opening remarks, Hu drew sharp distinctions between Hong Kong's situation and any future reunification of Taiwan and China. He said Hong Kong had to accept the "one country, two systems" formula promised by Beijing in the absence of any viable alternatives.
"But Taiwan does have an alternative: it has the power to say 'no' to immediate annexation and to maintain its continuing democracy, freedom and prosperity," he said.
On the bright side, he said Hong Kong may ultimately serve as a "practical neutral ground of sorts that might lessen Beijing's allergy to the growth of democracy" on its soil.
Vowing to pursue "pragmatic diplomacy" despite Beijing's objections, Hu said Taiwan was not trying to "poke sticks in the gorilla's cage."
"We cannot do enough to stay out of trouble ourselves and we do not wish to cause trouble for anyone," he said. "What we do, we do for survival's sake."
